vignette:
The Weight of the Forest

Rajan is a 41-year-old South Asian man who has worked as a park ranger for nearly fifteen years. He loves his work with a quiet, steady devotion — the early mornings, the smell of pine and wet earth, the sense of being a custodian of something larger than himself. His partner, Meena, describes him as someone who used to bring that same calm attentiveness home with him. That version of Rajan feels, to both of them, like someone from a different life.

Three years ago, Rajan was taken captive during a routine patrol in a remote section of the park. A group of men — later identified as involved in illegal poaching operations — held him for eleven days in an isolated structure deep in the backcountry. He was bound, intermittently blindfolded, given minimal food and water, and subjected to repeated threats about what would happen if rangers or law enforcement came looking. He had no way of knowing whether anyone was searching for him, or whether he would survive. He tells it plainly now, as if recounting something that happened to a stranger, but his hands press flat against his thighs when he speaks, and he doesn't quite meet your eyes.

When he was found and released, the relief was immediate and enormous — and then, within days, it began to recede. He returned to work after six weeks because being home felt worse. The apartment felt small and airless in a way it never had before. He thought the forest would restore him. Instead, he found himself stopping on trails he had walked hundreds of times, certain that something was wrong, that he was being watched from the tree line. He began avoiding the remote sections of the park entirely, rerouting his patrols without fully acknowledging to himself what he was doing.

Sleep became its own ordeal. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart already hammering before he is fully conscious, the darkness of the bedroom briefly indistinguishable from the darkness of that room where he was held. He doesn't always remember a specific dream — sometimes it is just the feeling, a dense and suffocating dread, that takes an hour or more to fully lift. Meena has learned not to reach for him in those moments. Early on, he startled badly when she touched him in the dark, and the look on her face afterward — frightened, uncertain — is something he carries with him.

He is more irritable than he used to be, and he knows it. Small frustrations at work — a hiker who ignores a trail closure, a radio that cuts out — can produce a flash of anger that feels disproportionate even as he is feeling it. He apologizes afterward, but the apologies have started to feel hollow from repetition. He worries about what he is becoming.

There are days when he manages well. He still loves the work, or loves what the work used to mean to him, and he holds onto that. He is good with the seasonal staff — patient, knowledgeable, generous with his time. But there are also days when he sits in his truck at the trailhead for twenty minutes before he can make himself get out, running through a mental inventory of who else is in the park, where the nearest road is, whether his radio is fully charged. He tells himself this is just being prepared. He knows, on some level, that it is more than that.

He has not talked about any of this in detail with Meena, though she has asked. He doesn't want her to worry more than she already does, and he doesn't entirely trust that putting it into words won't make it more real. He comes to sessions with a kind of careful composure, the same composure he brings to the park — watchful, contained, already scanning for what might go wrong.
